artiest/mary-ford.text:
Mary Ford was born in 1924 as Iris Colleen Summers in El Monte, California. As a girl she sang in churches and made gospel recordings. In 1943 she formed the trio the Sunshine Girls with Vivian Earles and June Widener, who sang with Jimmy Wakely on the radio programme The Hollywood Barn Dance. In 1945 she met the guitarist Les Paul. They began performing together in 1946 and married at the end of 1949. In the meantime she had begun performing under the name Mary Ford: Paul picked that name from a telephone directory, because it had to be almost as short as his own.

With Les Paul she had a string of hits for Capitol Records in the first half of the 1950s. They included Tiger Rag, Mockin' Bird Hill, How High the Moon, Bye Bye Blues, The World Is Waiting for the Sunrise and Vaya con Dios, which spent eleven weeks at number one. How High the Moon stayed at the top for nine weeks. On these records Ford harmonised with herself: she sang the voices over one another, while Paul played the guitar and recorded multiple tracks.

The result sounded like a whole choir and a whole band, made by two people with a recording machine. In this way the duo became an example for those who later used multitrack recording to treat the studio as an instrument. Besides being a singer, she also played the guitar. The couple also presented radio programmes for NBC, such as Les Paul and Mary Ford at Home. Ford died in 1977.
artiest/mary-ford.listen: Listen to How High the Moon and try to count the voices: can you hear her as one singer accompanying herself, and what does Les Paul's guitar do in between?

artiest/mary-hopkin.text:
Mary Hopkin was born in 1950 in Pontardawe in Wales, into a Welsh-speaking family. She took singing lessons and began as a folk singer with a local group, the Selby Set and Mary. She recorded an EP of Welsh songs for the label Cambrian before signing with Apple Records, the Beatles' label. She was one of the first artists that Apple signed.

Paul McCartney produced her debut single Those Were the Days, which was released in August 1968 and reached number one in Great Britain. In the United States the record reached number two. Her debut album Post Card was released in February 1969, with songs by Donovan, George Martin and Harry Nilsson. The album reached number three in the British chart. The single Goodbye, written by McCartney, reached number two. Temma Harbour followed and, in 1970, Knock, Knock Who's There?, with which she represented the United Kingdom at the Eurovision Song Contest and came second. Think About Your Children was her last big hit in 1970.

Hopkin wanted to return to her folk roots and felt that she did so on Earth Song/Ocean Song from 1971, produced by Tony Visconti, whom she married. She has continued to release albums ever since, including Spirit in 1989 and Painting by Numbers in 2014. Her clear, restrained voice made her one of the gentle voices of the late 1960s, an example of what Apple also wanted to offer besides the Beatles.
artiest/mary-hopkin.listen: Listen to Those Were the Days and notice her voice: how clear and restrained she sings, and how does the accompaniment change as the song goes on?

artiest/mary-j-blige.text:
Mary J. Blige is an American singer from the Bronx in New York, born in 1971. At eighteen she signed with Uptown Records, as the label's youngest artist and first woman. She was nicknamed the Queen of Hip-Hop Soul, and that name says exactly what she did: she sang soul and R&B over the beats and samples of hip hop.

Her debut What's the 411? (1992) reached number 1 on the American R&B albums chart and went triple platinum. My Life (1994) followed, and with Share My World (1997) she topped the Billboard 200 for the first time. She later did so again with Love & Life (2003), The Breakthrough (2005) and Growing Pains (2007). The Breakthrough sold 727,000 copies in its first week, a record for a solo R&B singer. Her biggest single was Family Affair (2001), which spent six weeks at number 1 on the American Hot 100.

Blige won nine Grammys and in 2024 was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. She also acts in films; for Mudbound (2017) she received two Oscar nominations, for her role and for the song Mighty River. She was thereby the first person to be nominated in the same year for acting and for a song. In her music the singing tradition of soul and the sound of 1990s hip hop come together.
artiest/mary-j-blige.listen: Listen in Family Affair to how the beat by the producer Dr. Dre almost stands still on a short, repeated keyboard figure. Notice how Blige takes all the space above it: she sings, shouts and encourages, as if she were leading a party.

artiest/mary-lou-williams.text: Mary Lou Williams grew up in Pittsburgh and was already a professional pianist as a teenager. From 1929 she was pianist and arranger with Andy Kirk and His Twelve Clouds of Joy in Kansas City. Earl Hines was an important model for her piano playing. She wrote arrangements for Benny Goodman, Duke Ellington and Earl Hines. In the 1940s she moved to New York; her apartment in Harlem became a gathering place for young bebop musicians such as Thelonious Monk, Dizzy Gillespie and Bud Powell. She wrote the Zodiac Suite (1945), with twelve movements for the signs of the zodiac. Later she converted to Catholicism and wrote masses in jazz style. She is one of the few musicians who lived through all the styles from ragtime to free jazz.
artiest/mary-lou-williams.listen: Notice the riffs of the saxophones: Mary Lou Williams wrote that herself.

artiest/masabumi-kikuchi.text:
Masabumi Kikuchi was born in 1939 in Tokyo. After the bombing of the city in 1945 his family moved to the countryside of Aizuwakamatsu in Fukushima Prefecture, where his parents came from. He studied music at the Tokyo Art College High School and bought second-hand records, probably left behind by American soldiers. Duke Ellington, Miles Davis and Thelonious Monk were his first models. After his studies he played in Lionel Hampton's Japanese touring band and formed a quintet with Terumasa Hino. Soon afterwards he left for the United States with a scholarship to the Berklee College of Music.

He played with many different musicians, including Sonny Rollins, Miles Davis, McCoy Tyner, Elvin Jones, Gary Peacock and Paul Motian, and worked with Gil Evans and Tōru Takemitsu. His albums include Poo-Sun (1970), Susto (1981), Tethered Moon Play Kurt Weill (1995), Chansons d'Édith Piaf (1999) and Experiencing Tosca (2004). In this way he played both his own work and arrangements of chansons and classical themes.

Kikuchi was known for a style of playing all his own. He played the piano as an instrument full of space and silence, in which every note matters. He died in 2015 in New York, where he lived. He belongs to the Japanese jazz musicians who sought their own path between Tokyo and New York.
artiest/masabumi-kikuchi.listen: Listen to Dancing Mist and notice how Kikuchi lets his notes ring out. What space do you hear between the piano sounds, and which of the accompanists fills it?

artiest/masaru-sato.text: Masaru Sato was born in 1928 in Rumoi on Hokkaido. He studied at the National Academy of Music and became a pupil of Fumio Hayasaka at the film studio Toho. He helped with the orchestration of Shichinin no samurai (1954). After Hayasaka's sudden death in 1955 he took over the work for Akira Kurosawa. Among other things he wrote the music for Kumonosu-jō (Throne of Blood, 1957), Yōjimbō (1961) and Akahige (1965). Unlike Akira Ifukube, Sato used Western popular styles and light jazz. He also wrote for four Godzilla films, from Gojira no gyakushū (1955) to Godzilla vs. Mechagodzilla (1974). In 44 years at Toho he made more than 300 film scores. He wrote only for film, not for the concert hall.
artiest/masaru-sato.listen: Compare the menacing, austere sounds of Throne of Blood with the rough, almost comic theme of Yōjimbō, in which brass and percussion set the tone.

artiest/masato-nakamura.text:
Masato Nakamura was born in 1958 and is a Japanese bassist and producer. He began as a session musician and, with the singer Miwa Yoshida, formed a project that in 1988 grew into the J-pop band Dreams Come True, together with the keyboardist Takahiro Nishikawa. The band has sold more than fifty million CDs. In 2002 Nakamura and Yoshida founded their own record label, DCT Records. Nakamura writes a large share of the band's songs and does almost all the arrangements.

Outside Japan he is best known for his work for computer games. The company Sega chose him in early 1990 to make the music for the first Sonic the Hedgehog, which came out in 1991. Later that year the game was shown for the first time by being painted on the tour bus of Dreams Come True. He also made the music for the sequel, Sonic the Hedgehog 2 from 1992, while at the same time working on albums by his band. In 2006 he made a new version of the ending theme of the second game for a later Sonic game.

The music of Sonic belongs to the first generation of game music that also became popular outside the gaming world. Nakamura brought the melodic, smooth side of Japanese pop to the small sound chip of a game console. In this way he contributed to the sound that would later come to be called chiptune.
artiest/masato-nakamura.listen: Listen to Green Hill Zone and notice the cheerful melody that keeps returning and the fast bass line beneath it. Can you hear that the piece could just as well have been a pop song?

artiest/mason-williams.text:
Mason Williams was born in 1938 in Abilene, Texas, and grew up between Oklahoma and Oregon. He studied at Oklahoma City University and served in the American navy from 1961 to 1963. He became a classical guitarist, composer, singer, writer, comedian and poet, and in so doing a versatile figure in American television and music of the 1960s. His friendship with the artist Edward Ruscha dates from his years in Oklahoma.

His greatest success was Classical Gas, an instrumental piece from 1968 that appeared on The Mason Williams Phonograph Record. It won three Grammy Awards, including for the orchestral arrangements by Mike Post, and sold more than a million copies. For Warner Bros. he recorded five albums, including The Mason Williams Ear Show and Hand Made in 1970. For the covers of Hand Made and Sharepickers he received Grammy nominations. He also wrote songs for The Kingston Trio and, together with Nancy Ames, Cinderella Rockefella, a number one in Great Britain in 1968 for Esther and Abi Ofarim.

Outside music he worked as a writer for The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour, The Glen Campbell Goodtime Hour and Saturday Night Live. His music combines the technique of the classical guitar with folk and an orchestral sound, and shows how an instrumental piece could still rank high in the charts in the age of beat groups and protest singers. Classical Gas remained his trademark, with new versions in 1987, 2003 and 2005.
artiest/mason-williams.listen: Listen to Classical Gas and notice how the acoustic guitar carries the themes and how the orchestra joins in later in the piece.

artiest/massada.text:
Massada was a Dutch band with a background in funk, rock and pop and with Latin American influences. The group was founded by Johnny Manuhutu, and many members had Moluccan roots. Their models were groups such as Malo, Escena and El Chicano. They were compared with Santana early on, although at the time they did not yet know that band. From 1975 there were opportunities to record, but because of the terms the group turned those offers down.

In 1978 that changed. The debut album Astaganaga appeared that year, with the hit singles Latin Dance and Dansa (Don't Quit Dancing), both of which stayed in the chart for eight weeks. A book about this album later appeared in the 33⅓ series, written by Lutgard Mutsaers. In 1979 came Unknown Destination and the album Pukul Tifa. In 1980 Sajang é reached number one in the Dutch Cash Box chart, alongside hits such as Feelin' Lonely and I Never Had A Love Like This Before. The album Pusaka appeared in 1980, Baru in 1981. In 1986 they also covered Vahevala, a hit by Loggins and Messina from 1972.

Massada showed how Dutch pop music could mix with Moluccan and Latin influences, with percussion, guitars and danceable rhythms. Fifty years after its founding, the group got together again in September 2023 for an anniversary tour, led by Johnny Manuhutu as singer and percussionist.
artiest/massada.listen: Listen to Latin Dance and notice the percussion and the guitar: which rhythms do you hear that you would not expect from an ordinary Dutch pop band?

artiest/massimo-palombella.text:
Massimo Palombella was born in 1967 in Turin and is an Italian priest and choral conductor. He joined the Salesians of Don Bosco and was ordained a priest in 1995. Alongside his studies of philosophy and theology at the Pontifical Salesian University he studied musicology at the Turin conservatory. He then worked in Rome in student chaplaincy and founded the Roman Interuniversity Choir, which he led as its first conductor. From 1995 he provided the music for the Pope's meetings with the Roman university community.

In October 2010 Pope Benedict XVI appointed him musical director of the Sistine Chapel Choir, the Cappella Musicale Pontificia Sistina, as successor to Giuseppe Liberto. That choir had previously been led by Domenico Bartolucci and Lorenzo Perosi. In 2017 Pope Francis made him an adviser to the Congregation for Divine Worship. He led the choir for eight years. At the end of 2024 he was ordered to repay 127,000 euros that he is alleged to have taken from the choir.

With the Sistine choir he recorded, among others, Palestrina in 2016, Veni Domine: Advent & Christmas at the Sistine Chapel in 2017 and O crux benedicta: Lent and Holy Week at the Sistine Chapel in 2019. Those recordings bring centuries-old church music, such as the polyphony of Palestrina, to a large audience of listeners outside the church.
artiest/massimo-palombella.listen: Listen to a piece by Palestrina on the album of that name and notice how the voices enter in turn and weave through one another, without instruments.

artiest/massive-attack.text:
Massive Attack is an English group from Bristol, founded in 1988 by Robert Del Naja (3D), Grant Marshall (Daddy G), Adrian Thaws (Tricky) and Andrew Vowles (Mushroom). The four knew one another from The Wild Bunch, one of the first British sound systems, which dominated the clubs of Bristol in the mid-1980s. There they mixed hip hop, soul and reggae together, and that mix became the basis of their own music.

In 1991 the debut album Blue Lines appeared, made with the help of Neneh Cherry and her partner Cameron McVey and partly recorded in their house. The album is regarded as the first trip hop record: slow, dark beats, bass lines from reggae, samples and guest singers such as Horace Andy and Shara Nelson, alternating with the half-spoken raps of the group members themselves. The single Unfinished Sympathy, with strings recorded in the Abbey Road studio, reached number 1 in the Netherlands. Because of the Gulf War the group briefly called itself simply Massive.

After Protection (1994) Tricky left for a solo career. Mezzanine (1998), with Teardrop, became their first number 1 album in the United Kingdom and sounded heavier and darker. Del Naja and Marshall then continued as a duo. Together with Portishead and Tricky, Massive Attack defined the sound of Bristol in the 1990s and showed that dance music can also be slow, sombre and atmospheric.
artiest/massive-attack.listen: Listen to Unfinished Sympathy and notice how the strings, the beat and the voice of Shara Nelson together build tension. Hear how the tempo stays calm while the song still grows ever fuller.

artiest/matmos.text:
Matmos is an American electronic duo, formed in San Francisco and now based in Baltimore. The core consists of M. C. Schmidt and Drew Daniel, who are also a couple. The name comes from the science fiction film Barbarella (1968), in which Matmos is a lake of malevolent slime. The duo often works with guest musicians and released records on Matador and later on Thrill Jockey.

Matmos makes music from unusual sound sources. On the first album, Matmos (1997), you can hear, among other things, freshly cut hair and the amplified nerve activity of crayfish. For A Chance to Cut Is a Chance to Cure (2001) the duo recorded sounds from surgical operations and reworked them into melodic pieces of experimental techno. Other albums are The Civil War (2003), The Rose Has Teeth in the Mouth of a Beast (2006), Plastic Anniversary (2019) and Metallic Life Review (2025). Return to Archive (2023) they made for the 75th anniversary of the archive Smithsonian Folkways, with reworked field recordings from that collection.

For pop history Matmos matters above all because of the collaboration with Björk. The duo remixed her single Alarm Call in 1998, then contributed to the albums Vespertine (2001) and Medúlla (2004) and played on her tours. On Vespertine small, crackling sounds are the building blocks of the beats. Who exactly made what later became a matter of dispute: Björk said that she had made most of the beats herself, but that the credit often went to Matmos.
artiest/matmos.listen: Listen in Hidden Place by Björk, from the album Vespertine, to the beat: no drum kit, but small ticks, rustling and crackling sounds. Notice how the choir and the strings float above it, while the rhythm stays small and close.

artiest/matt-aitken.text:
Matt Aitken is an English songwriter and producer. He was born in 1956 and grew up in Astley, near Manchester. He began as a guitarist and played in all kinds of bands and on cruise ships, where he learned to adapt to any style of music. Around 1980 Mike Stock brought him into his band. The two bought a mixing desk and a tape recorder, and from January 1984 they worked only in the studio, as writers and producers for others. That same year they joined forces with Pete Waterman. Thus Stock Aitken Waterman, SAW for short, came into being.

The trio began at small labels in Hi-NRG, the fast dance music of the gay clubs. In 1985 came the first number 1 hit, You Spin Me Round (Like a Record) by Dead or Alive. They then built their own studio in the Borough in south London, which was called the Hit Factory. There hits were made for Bananarama, Mel and Kim, Rick Astley, Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan. The songs had a fixed formula: a tight electronic beat, synthesizers and a cheerful melody that stuck immediately. Aitken played guitar and keyboards and helped with the writing and the production. According to Waterman he was a perfectionist, especially when it came to his guitar solos.

In 1991 Aitken left the trio. He spent a few years looking after his daughters and took up motor racing. In 1994 he started again with Mike Stock and had success with, among others, Nicki French, Scooch and Robson & Jerome. Around 2002 he withdrew from music again.
artiest/matt-aitken.listen: Listen to You Spin Me Round (Like a Record) by Dead or Alive, SAW's first number 1 hit. Notice the fast, pumping synthesizer bass and the hard electronic drums.

artiest/matt-bellamy.text:
Matt Bellamy is the singer, guitarist, pianist and lyricist of the British rock band Muse. He was born in 1978 in Cambridge and grew up in Teignmouth, a seaside town in Devon. At school he played in bands with the drummer Dominic Howard; the bassist Chris Wolstenholme joined, and in 1994 the trio called itself Muse.

The debut Showbiz appeared in 1999. It was followed by, among others, Origin of Symmetry (2001), Absolution (2003), Black Holes and Revelations (2006) and The Resistance (2009), with songs such as Plug In Baby, Supermassive Black Hole, Knights of Cydonia and Uprising. Muse won two Grammys for best rock album, for The Resistance and Drones (2015). The music mixes heavy guitar rock with influences from Romantic classical music: piano parts, broad melodies and sometimes a whole orchestra, as in Butterflies and Hurricanes.

Bellamy has a tenor voice with a wide range. He sings with vibrato and falsetto and stretches syllables over several notes, something he partly took from Jeff Buckley. On the guitar he uses effects that make the instrument sound like a synthesizer, such as fuzz, arpeggiators and pitch shifters. His guitars, built by Manson, have built-in effects and a touch panel with which he can control sounds; in 2019 he bought a majority stake in that company. Besides Muse he wrote, with Ilan Eshkeri, music for a radio play of 1984 and for the television series MobLand (2025).
artiest/matt-bellamy.listen: Listen in Muscle Museum to how the song alternates between restrained verses and loud outbursts of guitar and drums. Notice the moment when Bellamy launches into his high falsetto in the chorus.

artiest/matt-rowe.text:
Matt Rowe is a British songwriter and producer. In the 1990s he formed a songwriting duo with Richard Stannard, which wrote and produced pop songs in London. There is little to be found in the usual sources about Rowe's own background; his name is linked mainly with one group: the Spice Girls.

Stannard saw the five singers at a showcase in the Nomis Studios at the end of 1994 and told Rowe that he had found the pop group of their dreams. From January 1995 the two wrote songs together with the group. In December 1995 they recorded Wannabe at the Strongroom in London. Rowe put the drum loop together on his MPC3000 drum machine; the five added shouted, rapped and sung sections, which were stuck together as cut-and-paste work. The song was written in about half an hour and recorded in less than an hour. Rowe also played keyboards and co-wrote the lyrics.

Wannabe was released in the summer of 1996. It spent seven weeks at number 1 in England and by the end of 1997 had reached number 1 in 37 countries, including America. In 1997 it won an Ivor Novello Award and a Brit Award. Rowe and Stannard also wrote the ballad 2 Become 1 and Mama with the group. Rowe felt that all five Spice Girls contributed equally to the songs. His work shows how a pop group and a regular team of writers together could make a worldwide hit in a short time.
artiest/matt-rowe.listen: Listen in Wannabe to Rowe's drum loop: a skipping rhythm at 110 bpm, in which Stannard heard something of the rock 'n' roll from Grease. Notice how the shouted, rapped and sung sections are stuck one after another as separate blocks.

artiest/matthew-fisher.text:
Matthew Fisher is an English organist, born in 1946 in Croydon, near London. He is best known as the organist of Procol Harum, the group he joined in early 1967. That same year A Whiter Shade of Pale appeared, which spent weeks at number 1 in England. Fisher played the Hammond part, with the famous melody in the intro and the solos between the verses.

At the end of 1969 Fisher left the group. He became a producer, including for the guitarist Robin Trower, whose albums Bridge of Sighs and For Earth Below went gold in America. He also made solo records, such as Journey's End (1973) and I'll Be There (1974). From 1991 to 2004 he played with Procol Harum again. After a degree at Cambridge he became a computer programmer in 1995.

Fisher felt that he should be named as a co-writer of A Whiter Shade of Pale, because the organ part was so defining. The other writers refused. In 2006 the London High Court ruled that he was a co-author and awarded him 40 per cent of the composer's share. On appeal he received no money, because he had waited too long with his claim, but in 2009 the House of Lords restored the first ruling: under English copyright law there is no time limit for such a claim. The case shows that an instrumental part can be just as much a part of a composition as the melody and the lyrics.
artiest/matthew-fisher.listen: Listen to the beginning of A Whiter Shade of Pale: Fisher's Hammond melody sounds first on its own, with bass and drums, before the vocals begin. Notice how that melody returns between the verses and how the bass line quietly descends beneath it.

artiest/matthews-southern-comfort.text:
Matthews Southern Comfort is a British group that plays country rock and folk rock. The singer Iain Matthews, who had previously been in Fairport Convention, started the band in 1970 so that he could go on tour with his solo album Matthews' Southern Comfort. The band included, among others, the guitarists Mark Griffiths and Carl Barnwell and Gordon Huntley on pedal steel, the guitar that lies flat and makes the gliding country sound. The group became known for its three-part harmony singing.

Still in 1970 the albums Second Spring and Later That Same Year followed. The breakthrough came with a version of Woodstock by Joni Mitchell, first played for a session at the BBC. The single was released in July 1970 and reached number 1 in England in October. In America the version by Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young was more successful. Where they turned it into an electric rock number, Matthews Southern Comfort opted for a calm, gentle performance.

Matthews did not enjoy the success. He had no desire for media attention and did not want to be labelled a country rocker. In November 1970 he quit, just before a gig in Birmingham. The others carried on as Southern Comfort, while Matthews began a long solo career in America. Since 2010 the name has existed again, with mainly Dutch musicians; Kind of New (2010), Like a Radio (2018) and The New Mine (2020) have appeared in this way.
artiest/matthews-southern-comfort.listen: Listen in Woodstock to the pedal steel of Gordon Huntley, which lies like a soft wave beneath the vocals, and to the harmonies in the chorus. Then compare it with the much more powerful version by Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young.

artiest/maurice-jarre.text: Maurice Jarre was born in 1924 in Lyon and studied at the Paris conservatoire, with percussion as his main subject. For years he worked for Jean Vilar's theatre. After French films such as Les yeux sans visage (1960), the director David Lean asked him for Lawrence of Arabia (1962). Jarre wrote a grand, broad theme and used unusual colours such as the ondes Martenot, an early electronic instrument. It earned him an Oscar, as did Doctor Zhivago (1965), in which Lara's theme became world famous with balalaikas. In the 1980s he switched to synthesizers, as in Witness (1985). He won three Oscars, all three for films by Lean.
artiest/maurice-jarre.listen: Notice the broad main theme with its great leaps, and hear how percussion and unusual instruments colour the desert or the Russian steppe.

artiest/maurice-jaubert.text: Maurice Jaubert, from Nice, was the most important film composer of French poetic realism. He worked with Jean Vigo, René Clair, Julien Duvivier and Marcel Carné. Jaubert felt that film music should not underline every emotion. It had to give the film a rhythm and atmosphere of its own. For Zéro de conduite (1933) he played a piece backwards under a slowed-down scene, so that the sound became unreal. In L'Atalante (1934) and Le quai des brumes (1938) small ensembles, waltzes and street songs can be heard. Jaubert was killed in action at the front in June 1940. François Truffaut later reused his music in four of his films.
artiest/maurice-jaubert.listen: Notice the sparse instrumentation and the little waltzes and song melodies that create atmosphere without echoing the images.

artiest/maurice-ravel.text: Maurice Ravel was born in the Basque town of Ciboure and worked all his life in and around Paris. He was a master of orchestration and wrote clear, precisely finished music, with influences from Spanish dance, old French forms and, later, jazz. His Boléro from 1928 repeats two melodies over an unchanging drum rhythm, while the orchestra grows steadily fuller. He himself called it an experiment: orchestral fabric without music.
artiest/maurice-ravel.listen: Listen to the beginning of the Boléro and hear how the snare drum quietly sets up a steady rhythm, after which the flute takes over the melody.

artiest/maurice-white.text:
Maurice White was the founder, leader and chief producer of Earth, Wind & Fire. He was born in 1941 in Memphis and studied at the conservatory in Chicago. There he worked as a studio drummer at Chess Records, including on records by Etta James and Chuck Berry. In 1966 he became drummer of the Ramsey Lewis Trio. On the album Another Voyage (1969) he played the kalimba, an African thumb piano, for the first time.

In 1969 White started the group Salty Peppers in Chicago. After a move to Los Angeles he called the band Earth, Wind & Fire. White wrote most of the songs and sang the lead parts together with Philip Bailey. He added a full horn section, first the Phenix Horns and later the Earth, Wind & Fire Horns. This created funk with the fullness of a big orchestra: brass, percussion, multi-part vocals and the kalimba as a special colour. Boogie Wonderland (1979), with the vocal group The Emotions, reached the top 10 in America. As a producer White also made Best of My Love by The Emotions, which reached number 1 in 1977.

The albums of Earth, Wind & Fire have sold more than 90 million copies in total. White won seven Grammys, was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the band and was himself inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. He suffered from Parkinson's disease for a long time and died in 2016 in Los Angeles, aged 74.
artiest/maurice-white.listen: Listen in Boogie Wonderland to the brass: short, fierce stabs that answer the vocals. Notice too how the voices of Earth, Wind & Fire and The Emotions alternate above the disco beat.

artiest/maurizio-bassi.text:
Maurizio Bassi is an Italian musician, keyboardist and producer from Milan. In the mid-1980s he was looking for new talent for a project of his own. This is how Baltimora came about in Milan, with the Northern Irish singer and dancer Jimmy McShane from Derry as its face. Bassi wrote most of the songs together with the American lyricist Naimy Hackett, brought in session musicians for the first album and played the keyboards himself.

In April 1985 Tarzan Boy was released, a cheerful Italo disco single with a jungle cry in the chorus. The song reached the top 5 in many European countries and in August 1985 reached number three in England. In America it reached number 13 in early 1986. Woody Boogie followed, and the albums Living in the Background (1985) and Survivor in Love (1987). In 1987 the project came to an end; McShane died in 1995.

A rumour has long surrounded the vocals on the records. According to some sources Bassi sang in the studio, but not at live performances, and McShane mimed on stage to a voice that was not his own. The Italo disco producer Tom Hooker has also claimed that Bassi did the lead vocals. The story fits the dance music of those years, in which producers made the music and someone else became the face. Besides Baltimora, Bassi worked with Italian artists such as Eros Ramazzotti, Matia Bazar and Pupo. In 1989 he won the Targa Tenco for best song with Se me lo dicevi prima, which he wrote with Enzo Jannacci.
artiest/maurizio-bassi.listen: Listen in Tarzan Boy to the jungle cry in the chorus and the bright synthesizer melody that keeps coming back. Then notice the voice in the verses: do you hear the man from the video clip, or the producer behind the controls?

artiest/maurizio-pollini.text:
Maurizio Pollini was born in 1942 in Milan and became one of the great Italian pianists of his time. His father was an architect and amateur violinist, his mother had studied to be a pianist and singer. He was taught by Carlo Lonati and then by Carlo Vidusso at the Milan conservatory. At fifteen he made his debut with études by Chopin. In 1957 he came second at the Geneva competition, after Martha Argerich, and in 1960 he won the International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw. After that he did not perform for a year and kept on studying. In the early 1960s he also worked for half a year with Arturo Benedetti Michelangeli.

His recordings span a wide repertoire: Chopin, Beethoven, Schubert, Debussy and the Second Viennese School, with records such as Études op. 10 and op. 25 from 1973 and Schoenberg: The Piano Music from 1975. He also played new music by Pierre Boulez, Karlheinz Stockhausen and Luigi Nono, and felt that contemporary composers belonged in concert life. Nono, for example, wrote a piece for him in 1974 and 1976. His playing was known for technique and control, although some found it dry and cerebral in his early years.

In the 1960s and 1970s Pollini was also active on the left, together with Claudio Abbado and Luigi Nono, but he kept politics and music apart. In 1968 he made his debut at Carnegie Hall, and in 1974 he toured Japan for the first time. He died in 2024. He showed that a pianist from the classical tradition could build a bridge to the music of his own time.
artiest/maurizio-pollini.listen: Listen to a Chopin étude from Études op. 10 and notice the speed and evenness of the right hand: can you hear how much control it takes to make that sound so calm?

artiest/max-martin.text:
Max Martin was born in 1971 as Karl Martin Sandberg in Sweden and grew up in Stenhamra, close to Stockholm. He is a songwriter and producer, not an artist on stage. Even so, he co-wrote more number 1 hits in the American Billboard Hot 100 than anyone except Paul McCartney. In March 2024, with his twenty-seventh number 1, he caught up with John Lennon.

In the 1980s he sang in the Swedish glam metal band It's Alive. In 1993 the producer Denniz PoP brought him to the Cheiron Studio in Stockholm, where a group of young writers and producers made hits. Denniz PoP also gave him his artist name. After PoP's death in 1998 Martin became the leader of the studio. From Stockholm came the hits of a new generation of American teen stars: ...Baby One More Time (1998) by Britney Spears, I Want It That Way (1999) by the Backstreet Boys and It's Gonna Be Me (2000) by *NSYNC. Cheiron closed in 2000. Martin continued with a studio of his own and wrote and produced for Katy Perry, Ariana Grande, The Weeknd and Taylor Swift. With Swift and Shellback he made Shake It Off (2014). Blinding Lights (2019) by The Weeknd, which he co-wrote, is regarded as the most successful song in the history of the Hot 100.

Martin works like the hit factories before him: Tin Pan Alley, the Brill Building, Motown and Stock Aitken Waterman. A team makes the music, and the singer drops by to sing in their part. His colleague Savan Kotecha summed up his method: melody first. The lyrics mainly have to sound good.
artiest/max-martin.listen: There is no excerpt under Max Martin's own name; listen to I Want It That Way by the Backstreet Boys, which he wrote with Andreas Carlsson. Notice how the hook ends on the word 'way', an open 'ay' sound that the singers can hold for a long time. A vowel like that sings well, even though, according to the group themselves, the lyrics do not quite make sense.

artiest/max-richter.text: Max Richter was born in 1966 in Germany and grew up in England. He studied in London and in Florence with Luciano Berio. His style combines minimal music with electronics and a romantic, melancholy sound. The album The Blue Notebooks (2004) made him known, and the piece 'On the Nature of Daylight' from it turned up in numerous films, such as Arrival (2016). For the animated documentary Waltz with Bashir (2008) he wrote slow, desolate music about memories of war. The HBO series The Leftovers (2014) was given strings and piano that express grief and loss. For Ad Astra (2019) he combined synthesizers and orchestra. Long, slowly blossoming chords are his signature.
artiest/max-richter.listen: Listen to the long, slow string chords and how a simple harmonic sequence gains more and more weight through repetition.

artiest/max-roach.text: Max Roach grew up in Brooklyn and as a teenager was already playing at Minton's and Monroe's Uptown House. He built on the work of Kenny Clarke and became the most important drummer of bebop. He played with Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and from 1954 led a leading quintet with the trumpeter Clifford Brown. Roach saw the drum kit as a melodic instrument and played solos with a clear shape. After Brown's death in 1956 he committed himself more and more to the civil rights movement. In 1960 he recorded We Insist! Max Roach's Freedom Now Suite with the singer Abbey Lincoln. Later he taught at university and worked with hip hop musicians.
artiest/max-roach.listen: Hear how the drum solo has a clear shape, with themes that return.

artiest/max-steiner.text: Max Steiner was born in Vienna in 1888. By his own account he still received lessons from Gustav Mahler, and he worked as an operetta conductor in Europe and on Broadway. In 1929 he came to Hollywood. With King Kong (1933) he showed what a continuous orchestral score can do: the music builds tension, sketches the island and gives the monster a theme of its own. Steiner followed the action closely and gave characters leitmotifs. He wrote well over three hundred scores, mainly for Warner Bros. Well known are Gone with the Wind (1939) with the Tara theme, Casablanca (1942) and the Western The Searchers (1956). He is often called the father of Hollywood film music.
artiest/max-steiner.listen: Notice how the music follows every movement and mood, and how a character returns with his own theme.

artiest/maxene-andrews.text:
Maxene Andrews was born in 1916 and was the soprano of the Andrews Sisters, an American vocal group from the swing and boogie-woogie era. Together with her sisters LaVerne, the alto, and Patty, the mezzo-soprano who sang lead, she grew into one of the most popular groups of her time. They began as imitators of the Boswell Sisters, performed with dance orchestras and in vaudeville, and came to national attention in 1937 with recordings and radio broadcasts. Their arranger Vic Schoen and the founders of Decca Records, Jack and David Kapp, had a large share in that.

In the years of the Second World War the sisters had hit after hit, also together with Bing Crosby. Their hit from 1941, Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy, has remained the best known. They performed for Allied troops in Africa, Italy and the United States, recorded V-Discs for the armed forces and sang Any Bonds Today? to sell war bonds. The tight close harmony of three voices, the swinging rhythms and the boogie-woogie bass became their trademark.

After LaVerne's death in 1967 Maxene and Patty parted ways. Maxene became a college dean and taught troubled young people. When Bette Midler covered Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy in 1972, attention returned, and in 1973 the sisters appeared on Broadway in the musical Over Here! In 1993 her album Maxene: An Andrews Sister appeared. She died in 1995. The Andrews Sisters were later inducted into the Vocal Group Hall of Fame and their style has been imitated by others, from Bette Midler to Pentatonix.
artiest/maxene-andrews.listen: Listen to Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy and notice how the three voices sing as a single whole: who has the melody, and how does the rhythm of the accompaniment speed up?

artiest/may-aufderheide.text:
May Aufderheide was born in 1888 and was an American ragtime composer. She is probably the best-known woman among ragtime composers. She had received a classical musical education and made a grand tour of Europe, but still chose to write ragtime. She belonged to the ragtime community of Indianapolis, which also included Paul Pratt, J. Russel Robinson, Will B. Morrison, Julia Lee Niebergall and Gladys Yelvington.

Her first published rag, Dusty, appeared in 1908. Its success convinced her father, the financier John H. Aufderheide, to start a music publishing house, J. H. Aufderheide Music Publisher. She then composed and published Richmond Rag, The Thriller, Buzzer Rag, Blue Ribbon Rag, A Totally Different Rag and Novelty Rag, besides waltzes and songs such as I'll Pledge My Heart To You. A song version of A Totally Different Rag also appeared, with lyrics by Earle C. Jones. With others she wrote songs such as I Want A Patriotic Girl and I Want A Real Lovin' Man.

In 1908 she married the architect Thomas M. Kaufman and moved to Richmond, Indiana. Because of problems in the family she stopped publishing early. In 1947 the family left for California. Aufderheide died in 1972 in Pasadena. She was one of the first women to turn the rhythm of piano music into a composition of its own in ragtime, at a time when that genre was still mostly written by men.
artiest/may-aufderheide.listen: Listen to Dusty Rag and notice how the left hand plays a steady, marching rhythm while the right hand dances over it with shifted accents.

artiest/mc-solaar.text:
MC Solaar is the artist name of Claude M'Barali, born in 1969 in Dakar to parents from Chad. When he was six months old the family moved to the Paris suburbs, including Saint-Denis and Villeneuve-Saint-Georges. At twelve he lived for nine months with an uncle in Cairo. He studied languages and philosophy and released his first single in 1990. In the summer of 1991 he went to Paris with his friend Jimmy Jay, and success came quickly with Bouge de là, based on a sample of The Message by Cymande.

His debut album Qui sème le vent récolte le tempo appeared at the end of 1991 and sold more than four hundred thousand copies in France. In 1994 Prose Combat followed, which sold a hundred thousand copies in its first week and became a bestseller in twenty other countries. In 1995 he received a Victoire de la Musique. Paradisiaque followed in 1997, Cinquième as in 2001, Mach 6 in 2003 and Chapitre 7 in 2007. Outside France he signed with the London acid jazz label Talkin' Loud and recorded with Urban Species and with Guru of Gang Starr.

His rap is fluid, full of wordplay and questions, over supple, jazzy grooves, often with Jimmy Jay as producer. In his lyrics he wrote about Black immigrants in France and about his own roots. He is regarded as one of the most influential hip hop artists of France and showed that French rap could be literary and danceable at the same time.
artiest/mc-solaar.listen: Listen to Bouge de là and notice the way the rap glides over the sample: can you hear how the rhythm of the words and the rhymes drives the song?

artiest/mccoy-tyner.text: The pianist McCoy Tyner grew up in Philadelphia; Bud Powell and Thelonious Monk were his models. From 1960 to 1965 he played in John Coltrane's quartet. He used chords built on fourths instead of thirds: quartal chords. These sound open and hard and suit modal music. With his left hand he played powerful low root notes. After Coltrane he led groups of his own; The Real McCoy (1967) became a classic. His way of playing influenced nearly every jazz pianist after him.
artiest/mccoy-tyner.listen: Listen to the open, hard chords and the heavy bass notes in the left hand.

artiest/meade-lux-lewis.text:
Meade Lux Lewis was born in 1905, probably in Chicago, and grew into one of the best-known boogie-woogie pianists. As a boy he was influenced by the pianist Jimmy Yancey. His father, a guitarist who had made two records himself, introduced him to music and arranged violin lessons. After his father's death he gave up the violin at the age of sixteen and switched to the piano. He got the nickname Lux from childhood friends.

His best-known piece is Honky Tonk Train Blues. He first recorded it in 1927 for Paramount Records, and recorded it again in 1935 for Parlophone and in 1937 for Victor. With the left hand, the piece imitates the stamping rhythms of a train, while the right hand plays clear blues lines above it. Together with other boogie-woogie pianists he played for a long time at Café Society and toured as a trio. Their success inspired the founding of Blue Note Records in 1939 and set off a boogie-woogie craze lasting ten years, with swing arrangements by Tommy Dorsey and Will Bradley and later with country boogie and early rock 'n' roll.

In 1941 Lewis played celesta in Edmond Hall's Celeste Quartet. He appeared in the films New Orleans and Nightmare, and unnoticed in It's a Wonderful Life. He died in 1964 in a car accident in Minneapolis. Honky Tonk Train Blues has been recorded by many others, in large line-ups and on organ, and is also mentioned in books, including in the autobiography of Keith Richards.
artiest/meade-lux-lewis.listen: Listen to Honky Tonk Train Blues and try to hear the train: what does the left hand do, and how does the right hand imitate the sound of a wheel on the track?

artiest/meena-mangeshkar.text:
Meena Mangeshkar, later known as Meena Khadikar, was born in 1931 and is an Indian playback singer and composer who sings in Marathi and Hindi. She is the second daughter of Pandit Deenanath Mangeshkar and the sister of the singers Lata Mangeshkar, Asha Bhosle, Usha Mangeshkar and Hridaynath Mangeshkar. She thus comes from one of the best-known musical families of Indian film music.

In Hindi film she sang, among others, Duniya Mein Hum Aaye Hain To from Mother India, together with Lata and Usha Mangeshkar, Phagun aaya from Pilpili Saheb and the duet Aapne chheen liya dil with Mohammed Rafi in the film Farmaish. She also sang Hai mausam yeh mastaana from Aabroo and Are koi jaao ri piya ko bulao from Patrani.

She made her greatest name as a composer for the Marathi film industry. There she is best known for the children's song and children's album Asawa Sunder Chocolatecha Bungla, which was later also recorded in Bengali and Gujarati. The original version was sung by her children Yogesh and Rachna. Her song Saang Saang Bholanaath is also well known. In this way she shows that behind the big names of playback singing there were more musicians than just the front-row female singers, and that a family of singers could also produce composers.
artiest/meena-mangeshkar.listen: Listen to Duniya Mein Hum Aaye Hain To from Mother India and notice how the three voices of the sisters sound together and alternate.

artiest/mei-lanfang.text: Mei Lanfang, from Beijing, was the most famous performer of dan roles, the female roles in Peking opera that were then played by men. He made pieces such as The Drunken Concubine and Farewell My Concubine famous. In 1930 he toured the United States, and in 1935 Bertolt Brecht saw him perform, which influenced Brecht's idea of alienation. During the Japanese occupation he refused to perform.
artiest/mei-lanfang.listen: Listen to Farewell My Concubine and notice the high, tense head voice and the shrill jinghu fiddle that follows the singing closely.

artiest/mel-en-kim.text:
Mel & Kim were the London sisters Melanie and Kim Appleby. They signed with Supreme Records and ended up with Stock Aitken Waterman, the London producer trio behind many hits of the second half of the 1980s. Their sound leaned on house from Chicago, but with the trio's tight, cheerful pop production.

The first single, Showing Out (Get Fresh at the Weekend), reached number three in England in 1986 and was number 1 on the American dance chart. In 1987 came Respectable, which reached number 1 in England and sold more than 800,000 copies there. The album F.L.M. appeared in April 1987 and went platinum. The title song and That's the Way It Is (1988) also reached the top 10, so that every single by the duo became a top hit. In 1988 the sisters were nominated for a Brit Award as best new British act.

Behind the success lay an illness. Mel had been treated for a form of cancer in 1985, and in 1987 it returned in her spine. The sisters withdrew from publicity; Mel still recorded That's the Way It Is when she came out of hospital. Work on a second album stood still. On 18 January 1990 Mel died, aged 23. Kim then began a solo career and had two more top 10 hits, Don't Worry and G.L.A.D.
artiest/mel-en-kim.listen: Listen at the start of Respectable to the chopped-up voice fragments: the sisters are not singing there, their voices are cut into pieces and used as rhythm. Notice how those samples return later between the verses.

artiest/mel-lewis.text:
Mel Lewis was born in 1929 as Melvin Sokoloff in Buffalo, New York, the son of Russian-Jewish immigrants. He was already playing professionally as a teenager and in 1954 joined the orchestra of Stan Kenton. In 1957 he moved to Los Angeles, in 1963 to New York. He worked as a jazz drummer, session musician, teacher and writer and received fourteen nominations for a Grammy Award.

In 1966 he founded the Thad Jones/Mel Lewis Orchestra in New York with Thad Jones. The group began as informal jam sessions of the city's best studio and jazz musicians and then played every Monday night at the Village Vanguard. In 1979 the orchestra won a Grammy for the album Live in Munich. When Jones moved to Denmark in 1978, the group continued as Mel Lewis and the Jazz Orchestra. Lewis played with them on Mondays at the Vanguard until shortly before his death. Albums from his career include Jazz Mission to Moscow from 1962, The Big Band Sound of Thad Jones · Mel Lewis from 1968 and Mellifuous from 1995.

His cymbal work was regarded as unique. The drummer Buddy Rich said that Mel Lewis sounded like no one else, only like himself. He played Turkish cymbals of the Istanbul brand, light in weight and with a dark, rich sound. He died in 1990, shortly before his orchestra's twenty-fourth anniversary. That orchestra still plays at the Village Vanguard as the Vanguard Jazz Orchestra, and so shows how a big band can become a permanent home.
artiest/mel-lewis.listen: Listen to a big band recording by Thad Jones and Mel Lewis, such as The Big Band Sound of Thad Jones · Mel Lewis, and notice the cymbals: how dark and open does the ride sound, and how does Lewis keep the whole orchestra moving?

artiest/melanie-brown.text:
Melanie Brown, known as Mel B, is an English singer from Leeds, born in 1975. She became famous as Scary Spice of the Spice Girls, the best-selling girl group ever, with more than a hundred million records sold. She was one of the five singers who ended up in the group after auditions, and each of them was given a nickname and a type of her own.

In 1998, while the group still existed, she began a solo career. Her first single, I Want You Back, reached number 1 in England. The album Hot (2000) got no further than number 28, although the singles Tell Me and Feels So Good reached the top 5. The second album, L.A. State of Mind (2005), had little success: the single Today stalled at number 41.

After that Brown shifted her work to television. She came second in the American Dancing with the Stars (2007), sat on the judging panel of The X Factor in England and Australia and of America's Got Talent, and played Roxie Hart in the Broadway musical Chicago in 2016 and 2017. She wrote two memoirs, Catch a Fire (2002) and Brutally Honest (2018). In 2022 she was appointed MBE for her charity work. Her career shows how a member of a pop group builds an audience of her own after the group's success, with music as one element alongside television and books.
artiest/melanie-brown.listen: Listen to the opening of Wannabe: Mel B and Geri Halliwell talk and shout rather than sing. Notice how the voices of the five then keep taking over from one another, so that you hear each Spice Girl separately.

artiest/melanie-chisholm.text:
Melanie Chisholm, known as Melanie C or Mel C, is an English singer and songwriter. She was born in 1974 in Whiston and grew up in Widnes. After auditions she became one of the five Spice Girls, in which she was called Sporty Spice. With the group she sold more than a hundred million records.

As early as 1998 she made When You're Gone with Bryan Adams, which reached number three in England. Her first solo album, Northern Star (1999), produced two number 1 hits: Never Be the Same Again and I Turn to You. The album sold about four million copies worldwide.

After leaving Virgin she started a label of her own in 2004, Red Girl Records, on which she funded and released her records herself. In this way, among others, Beautiful Intentions (2005), This Time (2007), The Sea (2011), Version of Me (2016) and Melanie C (2020) appeared. Her ninth album, Sweat, reached number 3 in England in May 2026: her highest position as a solo artist and the highest of all the Spice Girls. In 2009 she appeared in the West End musical Blood Brothers, which earned her a nomination for a Laurence Olivier Award, and in 2022 her memoir Who I Am appeared. Chisholm is thus an example of a group member who, after the hype, built a long, independent career with a label of her own as its base.
artiest/melanie-chisholm.listen: Listen in Never Be the Same Again to the calm R&B beat and the rap verse by Lisa 'Left Eye' Lopes of TLC. Notice the contrast between Chisholm's soft, high singing and the fast, dry rap.

artiest/melba-liston.text:
Melba Liston was born in 1926 in Kansas City, Missouri. Her mother bought a trombone for her when she was seven, and she taught herself the instrument for the most part, with encouragement from her grandfather, a guitarist. At sixteen she joined the union for Black musicians, in order to take her first job in the orchestra of the Lincoln Theater. She played alongside Dexter Gordon and recorded with him in 1947. When Gerald Wilson's orchestra was disbanded in 1948, she went to Dizzy Gillespie. She was the first female trombonist to play alongside men in big bands from the 1940s to the 1960s.

In the 1950s she did other work for a time, including as an extra in Hollywood, and toured with Gillespie for the American State Department. In 1957 she recorded with Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers and in 1958 she formed a quintet of women. Her album Melba Liston and Her 'Bones appeared in 1959. She also worked for Milt Jackson, Clark Terry and Johnny Griffin, and wrote arrangements for Motown and for Marvin Gaye, Mary Lou Williams and Gloria Lynne.

Increasingly she became known as an arranger. She considered writing more important than soloing. Her collaboration with the pianist Randy Weston, which ran from the late 1950s, in particular produced a great deal of work for mid-sized and large ensembles. In Jamaica she composed, among other things, for the film Smile Orange and directed the music of The Dread Mikado. A stroke forced her to stop playing in 1985, but she carried on arranging. In 1987 she received a Jazz Masters Fellowship. She died in 1999.
artiest/melba-liston.listen: Listen to Melba Liston and Her 'Bones and notice how the trombones sound: an instrument that is usually in the background takes the lead here. Can you hear the lines she wrote as an arranger?

artiest/melle-mel.text:
Melle Mel, really Melvin Glover, is a rapper from the Bronx in New York, born in 1961. He was the lead rapper and main lyricist of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five. He was possibly the first rapper to call himself an MC, an abbreviation of master of ceremonies.

The group recorded for Enjoy Records and later for Sugar Hill Records, and first scored with party songs such as Freedom and The Birthday Party. Around 1982 Mel began writing about social subjects, such as the economic policy of President Reagan and drugs. The result was The Message (1982), which is often named as one of the first examples of conscious hip hop. Mel raps over an instrumental track by Duke Bootee; the other members of the Furious Five cannot be heard on the recording. The Message was later the first hip hop record to be added to the American National Recording Registry. White Lines (Don't Don't Do It), an anti-drugs song, followed.

With his rap in I Feel for You by Chaka Khan, Mel brought hip hop to a large R&B audience. In 1990 he won a Grammy for Back on the Block. In 2007 he and the Furious Five became the first rap group in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. His significance lies in a shift: from rap as party music to rap as a report on life in the city.
artiest/melle-mel.listen: Listen in The Message to the slow, heavy synthesizer groove over which Melle Mel tells his story, and to the chorus about someone on the edge. Notice the ending: the music runs on beneath an acted scene in which the group is arrested by the police.

artiest/melvin-van-peebles.text:
Melvin Van Peebles was born in 1932 in Chicago as Melvin Peebles. He studied literature at Ohio Wesleyan University and then served for over three years in the American air force. The Van in his name was added when he lived in the Netherlands in his late twenties. He worked as a cable car gripman in San Francisco, wrote a book about it and made short films. When he could not get work as a director in Hollywood, he moved to Europe, eventually to Paris.

In France he became a prolific writer of novels and plays. He wrote plays in French and used Sprechgesang, in which the text is spoken above the music. That style returned on his debut album Br'er Soul from 1968. In 1967 he made his first feature film, The Story of a Three-Day Pass, which was shot in France because it was hard for a Black American director to get work. In 1971 came his best-known film, Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song, in which he himself acted and for which he also made the music. The film led to the emergence of the blaxploitation genre. His play La Fête à Harlem became the musical Don't Play Us Cheap, of which an original cast album and soundtrack appeared in 1972. Ain't Supposed to Die a Natural Death, an album in 1970 and later a Broadway musical, also belongs here.

Van Peebles was an actor, filmmaker, writer and composer, and showed that a Black artist could produce his own stories and music himself. He died in 2021.
artiest/melvin-van-peebles.listen: Listen to a song from Br'er Soul and notice how he half speaks and half sings the lyrics: what does that do to the way you listen to the story?
